# Electromagnetic Vlasov–Maxwell kinetics {#sec-vlasov}

`apps/vlasov_maxwell` — a collisionless kinetic distribution function on a
three-dimensional phase space, coupled self-consistently to the full Maxwell
system, with a Lorentz cross-product force and electromagnetic instabilities.

Every other application in this report evolves a field over physical space.
This one evolves a *distribution over phase space*: the unknown is
$f_s(x, v_x, v_y, t)$, a function of one spatial and two velocity
coordinates, and the fields it is coupled to are three components of $E$ and
$B$ that live on the spatial line alone. The phase space is where the memory
goes and the coupling is where the physics is.

It is also the chapter where the reader meets a genuinely large system. That
is deliberate. @sec-alloy-dendrite showed that OpenPFC's finite-difference
and spectral stacks compose; this one shows that the framework survives a
problem whose unknown does not live on the grid the fields live on.

## Physical setting

A plasma is a gas in which the particles are charged, and that single change
makes it a field theory. Neutral gas molecules interact only when they
collide, so a neutral gas at low density is nearly a set of independent
particles. Charged particles interact through fields that every one of them
contributes to and every one of them feels, at every distance. A plasma is
therefore never a collection of particles in an external field; it is a
collection of particles in *its own* field, and that self-consistency is the
entire difficulty.

At the densities and temperatures where collisions can be neglected, the
statistical description is the **Vlasov equation**: the distribution function
$f_s(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}, t)$ is conserved along the trajectories of the
smooth, self-consistent field. Nothing is dissipated, nothing is lost, and
the entropy $-\int f \ln f$ is exactly constant. That makes the system
Hamiltonian in a strong sense — and it makes the two most famous phenomena in
the subject surprising.

**Landau damping.** A wave in a collisionless plasma decays. There is no
dissipation anywhere in the equations, entropy is exactly conserved, and yet
the electric field of a small perturbation dies away exponentially. The
energy is not lost; it goes into a progressively finer structure in velocity
space, carried by particles moving at close to the wave's phase velocity.
This is a real physical effect, it was predicted before it was measured, and
it is the sharpest test in this chapter because the damping rate is the root
of a transcendental equation that can be solved to machine precision and
compared against.

**Instability.** The same free energy that a Maxwellian has exhausted is
available whenever the distribution is *not* Maxwellian. Two counter-streaming
beams can give up their relative kinetic energy to a growing wave. Which wave
grows depends on the geometry, and the distinction matters here:

- Beams streaming **along** the wave vector drive a charge-density
  modulation. The unstable field is $E_x$, longitudinal; this is the
  electrostatic **two-stream** instability, and it is visible in a
  Vlasov–Poisson model with no magnetic field at all.
- Beams streaming **across** the wave vector drive a transverse current
  modulation. Current filaments of the same sign attract, the filaments
  coalesce, and the unstable field is a *magnetic* field $B_z$ that grows
  out of nothing. This is the **Weibel**, or filamentation, instability, and
  it cannot happen in an electrostatic model. It is why this application is
  electromagnetic and why it carries two velocity coordinates rather than
  one.

The second is the physically interesting case and the harder test. A model
that grows a magnetic field from a noise seed at the right rate has the
Lorentz force, the current deposition, the Maxwell update and the phase-space
transport all simultaneously correct; any one of them wrong and the growth
rate is wrong or the instability is absent.

## Governing equations

The complete system, presented before any reduction. For each species $s$
with charge $q_s$ and mass $m_s$:

$$
\frac{\partial f_s}{\partial t}
  + \mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f_s
  + \frac{q_s}{m_s}\left(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}\right)
      \cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{v}} f_s = 0
$$ {#eq-vm-vlasov}

coupled to Maxwell's equations,

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},
\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0,
$$ {#eq-vm-gauss}

$$
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = -\nabla\times\mathbf{E},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}
  = c^{2}\nabla\times\mathbf{B} - \frac{\mathbf{J}}{\varepsilon_0},
$$ {#eq-vm-maxwell}

and closed by the kinetic moments

$$
\rho(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s q_s \int f_s \,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v},
\qquad
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s q_s \int \mathbf{v}\, f_s \,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v}.
$$ {#eq-vm-moments}

@eq-vm-vlasov is one equation per species on a six-dimensional phase space;
@eq-vm-maxwell is six scalar evolution equations on physical space;
@eq-vm-gauss is two constraints; @eq-vm-moments is the coupling that makes
the whole thing self-consistent and nonlinear. Written out in components for
several species it is a system of a few dozen coupled equations, and that is
before a single discretisation choice is made.

### The 1D2V reduction, derived

The application solves a reduction, and the reduction is *derived* here
rather than substituted, because which components survive is not obvious and
getting it wrong is silent.

Take one spatial coordinate $x$, two velocity coordinates $(v_x, v_y)$, and
let every field depend on $x$ and $t$ only, so $\partial_y = \partial_z = 0$.
The closure $f_s(x, v_x, v_y, t)$ carries no $v_z$, so $J_z \equiv 0$.
Under those two statements @eq-vm-gauss and @eq-vm-maxwell separate into
three groups.

**One component disappears for free.** $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$ becomes
$\partial_x B_x = 0$, so $B_x$ is uniform in space; the $x$ component of
Faraday's law gives $\partial_t B_x = 0$, so it is uniform in time as well.
On a periodic line with $B_x(t=0) = 0$, therefore $B_x \equiv 0$ **exactly,
as an identity of the geometry**. This is worth stating clearly for a reason
that returns in @sec-vm-verification: it means $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$ is
*not* a meaningful numerical test in this geometry, and reporting it as a
passed check would be misleading.

**One pair decouples.** The remaining Faraday and Ampère components pair
$(E_z, B_y)$ together,
$\partial_t B_y = \partial_x E_z$ and
$\partial_t E_z = c^2 \partial_x B_y$, driven by $J_z$ — which the closure
has set to zero. That pair is a vacuum electromagnetic wave the plasma cannot
touch. Initialised to zero it stays zero, and the application does not carry
it.

**What is left is the physics.** Three field components,

$$
\partial_x E_x = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}
\qquad \text{(Gauss --- a constraint)}
$$ {#eq-vm-gauss1d}

$$
\frac{\partial E_x}{\partial t} = -\frac{J_x}{\varepsilon_0}
\qquad \text{(Ampère --- the evolution form of the same field)}
$$ {#eq-vm-ampere-x}

$$
\frac{\partial E_y}{\partial t} = -c^2\frac{\partial B_z}{\partial x}
   - \frac{J_y}{\varepsilon_0},
\qquad
\frac{\partial B_z}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial E_y}{\partial x} .
$$ {#eq-vm-transverse}

With $\mathbf{B} = B_z\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ and
$\mathbf{v} = (v_x, v_y, 0)$ the Lorentz force keeps its cross product
intact,

$$
(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})_x = +v_y B_z,
\qquad
(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})_y = -v_x B_z,
$$ {#eq-vm-lorentz}

which rotates velocity vectors in the $(v_x, v_y)$ plane at the gyro-frequency
$\omega_c = q_s B_z / m_s$. **That rotation is the whole reason for two
velocity coordinates.** A 1D1V model has no cross product, no gyro-motion, no
transverse current and therefore no electromagnetic instability; it is a
different and much easier problem.

### Normalisation

Time in $\omega_{pe}^{-1}$, length in the electron skin depth
$d_e = c/\omega_{pe}$, velocity in $c$, $E$ in $m_e c\,\omega_{pe}/e$, $B$ in
$m_e\omega_{pe}/e$, and $f_s$ scaled so $\int f_s\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v} =
n_s/n_0$. Then $c = \varepsilon_0 = 1$, and with $\sigma_s = q_s/(-e)$ and
$\mu_s = m_s/m_e$ the evolved system is

$$
\frac{\partial f_s}{\partial t}
 + v_x \frac{\partial f_s}{\partial x}
 + \frac{\sigma_s}{\mu_s}\left[
     \left(E_x + v_y B_z\right)\frac{\partial f_s}{\partial v_x}
   + \left(E_y - v_x B_z\right)\frac{\partial f_s}{\partial v_y}
   \right] = 0
$$ {#eq-vm-norm}

with @eq-vm-gauss1d–@eq-vm-transverse losing their $c$ and $\varepsilon_0$.
For electrons $\sigma_s = -1$, $\mu_s = 1$. The Debye length is
$\lambda_D = (v_{th}/c)\,d_e$, so electrostatic benchmarks quoted in
$k\lambda_D$ and electromagnetic ones quoted in $k d_e$ differ by the
thermal velocity in units of $c$.

### Gauss is a diagnostic, not a constraint to be imposed

@eq-vm-gauss1d and @eq-vm-ampere-x are two statements about the same field.
Differentiating the first in time and substituting the second,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\partial_x E_x - \rho\right)
  = -\left(\partial_x J_x + \partial_t \rho\right) = 0
$$ {#eq-vm-charge}

by the continuity equation, which is itself a moment of @eq-vm-vlasov.
**Gauss's law is preserved exactly if and only if the discrete scheme
conserves charge.** It is therefore not something to enforce and forget: it
is the sharpest available measurement of whether the transport and the
deposition are consistent with each other, and this application reports the
residual $\|\partial_x E_x - \rho\|_\infty/\|\rho\|_\infty$ at every
diagnostic sample of every run.

## Problem setup

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Use case | A collisionless electron plasma on a neutralising background, perturbed and allowed to evolve self-consistently with its own electromagnetic field. Five benchmark configurations, from a vacuum light wave to the Weibel instability |
| Domain | One OpenPFC 3-D `Domain` whose axes are $(x, v_x, v_y)$ — **the phase space is the grid.** $x$ spans $[0, L_x)$ in electron skin depths; $v_x$ and $v_y$ span $[-v_{\max}, +v_{\max}]$ in units of $c$ |
| Boundary conditions | $x$ **periodic**, physically. $v_x$, $v_y$ **not periodic**: zero inflow, and the distribution must be negligible at the boundary. The velocity boundary is the honest weak point of a structured-grid kinetic method, so the occupancy there is a reported diagnostic of every run rather than an assumption |
| Initial conditions | Analytic, in `ics.hpp`: Maxwellian, bi-Maxwellian, and two counter-streaming configurations that differ only in which velocity component carries the drift — along $k$ for the electrostatic two-stream case, across $k$ for the electromagnetic filamentation case |
| Key physical parameters | Per species $\sigma_s = q_s/(-e)$ and $\mu_s = m_s/m_e$; electrons are $(-1, 1)$. Thermal velocity $v_{th}/c$, drift $u/c$, box $L_x/d_e$, and the anisotropy $A = (v_{th,y}/v_{th,x})^2 - 1$ for the Weibel case. Ions are immobile by default and available as a second species behind a flag |
| Observables | Field energies $\tfrac12\int E_x^2$, $\tfrac12\int(E_y^2 + B_z^2)$; per-species particle number, momentum and kinetic energy; total energy; the Gauss residual; $\min f$; the $L^1$ and $L^2$ norms and the entropy $-\int f\ln f$; velocity-boundary occupancy |
| Model maturity | *(filled in from the measured results — see @sec-vm-verification)* |

### Numerical strategy

Strang splitting, and the reason it works so cleanly here is a property
specific to 1D2V electromagnetic Vlasov: **every split step is a
constant-coefficient translation along one axis.**

| step | equation | speed | independent of | method |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | $\partial_t f + v_x\,\partial_x f = 0$ | $v_x$ | $x$ | exact spectral shift, $\hat f_k \mapsto \hat f_k e^{-\mathrm{i}k v_x \Delta t}$ |
| B | $\partial_t f + a_x\,\partial_{v_x} f = 0$ | $a_x = \frac{\sigma}{\mu}(E_x + v_y B_z)$ | $v_x$ | semi-Lagrangian, Lagrange interpolation |
| C | $\partial_t f + a_y\,\partial_{v_y} f = 0$ | $a_y = \frac{\sigma}{\mu}(E_y - v_x B_z)$ | $v_y$ | semi-Lagrangian, over the distributed axis |

Step A is exact and carries no timestep restriction, because $x$ is periodic
and the shift speed does not depend on the coordinate being shifted. Steps B
and C are constant-coefficient for the same reason — $a_x$ depends on $x$
and $v_y$ but not on $v_x$, and $a_y$ depends on $x$ and $v_x$ but not on
$v_y$ — so each is a pure translation, not a variable-coefficient advection.
That is a real simplification and it is worth being explicit that it is a
property of this geometry rather than a general fact about Vlasov solvers.

**The field update is exact too.** In Fourier space along $x$ the
source-free transverse pair of @eq-vm-transverse is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}
\begin{pmatrix}\hat E_y\\ \hat B_z\end{pmatrix}
= -\mathrm{i}k
\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\hat E_y\\ \hat B_z\end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-vm-rot}

whose matrix exponential is the closed form
$\cos(k\Delta t)\,\mathbf{I} - \mathrm{i}\sin(k\Delta t)\,\mathbf{S}$ with $\mathbf{S} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
The light wave is therefore integrated **exactly, at any $\Delta t$**: it
carries no numerical dispersion and imposes no Courant condition, which for
an explicit electromagnetic solver is the restriction one would normally
expect to dominate. The current enters through Duhamel's formula, which is
the same exponential-time-differencing structure the spectral applications
of this report already use (@sec-etd).

What that leaves is worth saying plainly, because it is easy to present an
exact sub-step as though it made the method exact: the splitting is second
order, and **the real error of this application lives in the velocity-space
interpolation of steps B and C.** @sec-vm-verification measures it.

### Decomposition, and the cap it implies

The MPI decomposition is on $v_y$ **only**, and the consequences are the
reason for the choice:

- $x$ and $v_x$ are rank-local, so step A's transform is a local
  one-dimensional FFT needing no transpose, and step B is a purely local
  shift.
- Step C translates along the distributed axis and is served by the existing
  halo exchange, with width
  $\lceil \max|a_y|\,\Delta t/\Delta v_y\rceil + \tfrac12\,$(interpolation
  order). This is a Courant-like condition on the *velocity* step, checked at
  runtime: exceeding the halo is an error, never a silent wrap.
- $E_x$, $E_y$ and $B_z$ are one-dimensional in $x$ and cheap to replicate on
  every rank; the moments need one `MPI_Allreduce` per step over arrays of
  length $N_x$.
- **The rank count is capped at $N_{v_y}$.** That is a real limit of this
  decomposition and it is stated here rather than discovered during the
  scaling study. Going beyond it needs a second decomposition axis and a
  transpose, which is a larger change than this application justifies.

Memory is a first-class result rather than an implementation detail, and it
is the reason kinetic equations are expensive even though every operator in
@eq-vm-norm is first order: one species costs
$N_x N_{v_x} N_{v_y} \times 8$ bytes per working copy, so a
$1024\times512\times512$ phase space is 2.1 GB per copy before any field is
allocated. @sec-vm-scaling gives the measured figure.
